title: Baqi's elegy for Suleyman
greek: Ottoman Turkish Ey pay-bend-i dam-geh-i qayd-i nam u neng
short: Baqi's elegy (mersiye) for Sultan Suleyman I, who died in camp at Szigetvar in Hungary in September 1566, translated by E. J. W. Gibb (1882).
body: Baqi (1526-1600), called in his lifetime the 'sultan of poets', had won Suleyman's favour with a qasida in 1555; his elegy for the sultan is generally counted his masterpiece and one of the great poems of Ottoman literature, and Gibb reports that Von Hammer called it the most beautiful poem in the whole range of Ottoman literature. Suleyman, called the Magnificent in Europe and Kanuni ('the Lawgiver') in Turkey, died on the night of 6-7 September 1566 during the siege of Szigetvar. The first strophe, Gibb notes, is addressed to the reader: its first line ('O you, foot-bound in the snare of the trap of fame and shame') is a memento mori. 'Fool-bounden' is Gibb's coinage for a Turkish compound meaning 'fettered at the feet'.

title: The terkib-bend and its 'seven-fold verse'
short: The poem is a terkib-bend: strophes of seven couplets on one rhyme, each closed by a linking couplet on a new rhyme.
body: A terkib-bend is a strophic poem: each strophe (khane) consists of couplets on one rhyme, followed by a couplet with a different rhyme (the vasita or bend, 'tie') that links it to the next. Gibb's English version has seven strophes of seven rhyming couplets, each closed by such a couplet, and his 'seven-fold verse' refers, as his note 206 explains, to the seven rhyming couplets of each strophe. Gibb, who translated 'in the original forms', reproduces the scheme: each strophe has its own rhyme (snare / wear / share; great / state / gate; etc.) and ends on a couplet rhyming together (face / case). The linking couplets carry the most quotable lines of the poem.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

title: The dregs and the dust
short: Gibb explains that Persians throw away the lees after drinking: the body, at the end of life's banquet, is thrown to the dust like dregs.
body: Gibb's note 197 explains that the Persians throw aside the lees after drinking a cup of wine. The image fits the poem's governing metaphor of life as a feast that must end. 'The tulip-cheek' that must take 'the tint of autumn leaf' is the beautiful young face that turns yellow in age and death; in Ottoman lyric the red tulip is a figure of youth and of the wounded, blood-stained heart. The strophe's argument is that if even Suleyman died, the reader's pursuit of fame is foolish.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

anchor: the stone from hand of Fate
title: The stone in the beaker
short: A pebble thrown into a cup was the signal for a party to break up (Gibb's note 198): Fate ends the feast of life.
body: Gibb's note 198 states that a pebble thrown into a beaker is the signal for a party to break up, and cross-refers to another note in the volume. FitzGerald's first-edition opening of the Rubaiyat uses a related custom ('Morning in the Bowl of Night / Has flung the Stone that puts the Stars to Flight'), which FitzGerald glossed as the desert signal 'To Horse!'. In Baqi the stone also breaks the glass: joy's beaker is shattered by Fate. The image links the opening meditation to the drinking-party (bezm) imagery of Ottoman lyric.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

title: The charger and Rustem's Rakhsh
greek: Persian rakhsh ('lightning', name of Rustem's horse)
short: The word Gibb translates 'charger' is rakhsh, 'lightning', the name of the hero Rustem's horse in the Shahnama.
body: Gibb's note 199 explains that the word translated 'charger', rakhsh, 'lightning', was the name of the famous steed of Rustem, the national hero of Persia, whose adventures fill much of Firdawsi's Shahnama. The sultan is thus made a new Rustem, so mighty that earth's 'tourney-square' was too small for his horse's prancing. The couplet calls him 'Prince of Fortune's Cavaliers', and the one before 'war's Lion-Monarch', the sultan as warrior of the faith, the dominant image of the first half of the elegy.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Firdawsi, Shahnama, the story of Rustem and Rakhsh

title: The Magyar and the Frank
short: The Hungarians (Magyars) and the 'Franks' (western Europeans) were the enemies of Suleyman's campaigns, from Mohacs (1526) to Szigetvar (1566).
body: Suleyman's reign was marked by campaigns in central Europe: he took Belgrade (1521), destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohacs (1526), besieged Vienna (1529) and annexed central Hungary with Buda (1541). He died on his thirteenth campaign, at the siege of the Hungarian fortress of Szigetvar. 'Frank' (Turkish Frenk) is the general Ottoman word for western Europeans. The Turkish line plays on the sword's lustre and its 'dread gleaming', which Gibb renders with two different nouns, 'sword' and 'brand' (an archaic word for a sword).

title: Earth the Treasurer
short: The linking couplet: the sultan's face laid in the dust like a rose-leaf, and Earth storing him like a jewel in its casket.
body: The couplet that closes the first strophe turns burial into treasure-keeping: Earth is the treasurer who places the sultan in the grave as a jewel is laid in its case. The comparison of the face to a 'tender rose-leaf' laid gently down softens the warrior's portrait just drawn. Gibb renders the Turkish linking couplet with an English rhymed couplet (face / case), marking the formal break between strophes. The jewel image returns in the fourth strophe, where no pearl can ever equal the dead king.

title: Iskender and Dara
short: Suleyman is crowned like Iskender (Alexander the Great) and has armies like Dara (Darius), the last king of the Kayanian dynasty, as Gibb notes.
body: In Persian and Ottoman tradition Iskender (Alexander the Great) is the model world-conqueror, and Dara (Darius III) the last king of the ancient Iranian dynasty he defeated; Gibb's note 200 identifies Dara as Darius, the last monarch of the Keyani dynasty. Nizami's Iskendername and the Shahnama made both familiar. Comparing Suleyman to both the conqueror and the conquered emphasises sheer imperial grandeur. In the final strophe 'Iskender's couch of might' becomes the throne to which Selim succeeds.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Nizami, Iskandarnama (Book of Alexander)

anchor: with tears are filled their eyes
title: Tears at the sun: husn-i ta'lil
short: Gibb calls this a fine example of husn-i ta'lil: the tears caused by looking at the sun are ascribed to grief, since the sun recalls the sultan's face.
body: Husn-i ta'lil, 'beautiful explanation of cause', is the rhetorical figure of giving a poetic false cause for a natural fact. Gibb's note 202 explains: the tears that come when one looks at the sun are here ascribed to sorrow for the loss of the Sultan, whose glorious face the splendour of the sun recalls. It is the closing, linking couplet of the second strophe, and like the others it gathers the strophe's praise of the king's 'beauty fair, as sun and moon' into one memorable conceit.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpakli, eds., Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997)

title: The Judas-tree
short: The Judas-tree (erghavan) has vivid red-purple blossoms in spring; Baqi asks it to bloom 'gore-hued' in mourning.
body: The erghavan, the Judas-tree (Cercis siliquastrum), is often mentioned in Oriental poetry; it is common around Istanbul, where its purple-pink flowers cover the Bosphorus hills each spring before the leaves appear. Its colour makes it an emblem of blood and of passionate grief. The strophe is a sustained call for nature to mourn, a kind of pathetic fallacy: cloud weeps blood, stars rain tears, the sky changes its blue robe for black.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Oxford English Dictionary, 'Judas-tree, n.'

title: Heaven in mourning
short: The sky is asked to change its blue robe for black, and the world to wear mourning, in a universal funeral.
body: Black and dark blue were mourning colours in the Ottoman world, and the poet orders the whole cosmos to put them on. The 'robes of princely woe' are the mourning garments of a royal court. The strophe also mentions 'fairies and ... men' (peri and human), the two orders of beings who share the grief. Andrews and Kalpakli read Ottoman courtly poetry as a public performance of relationships of love and loyalty to the sultan; the elegy's universal mourning is the largest expression of such loyalty.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Walter G. Andrews and Mehmet Kalpakli, The Age of Beloveds: Love and the Beloved in Early-Modern Ottoman and European Culture and Society (Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 2005)

title: The huma
short: The huma is a fabulous bird of happiest omen: any head it overshadows will wear a crown, and it lives on bones alone (Gibb's note 203).
body: Gibb's note 203 describes the huma as a fabulous bird often mentioned in Eastern poetry, of the happiest augury: every head it overshadows will one day wear a crown; it also lives entirely on bones, never hurting any living creature. Baqi uses both traits: the sultan's soul flies up like a huma, and 'nought remaineth save a few bones on the earth below', bones being the huma's food. In the last strophe the 'Huma of high, happy flight' is the new sultan, Selim, on whom the bird's shadow now falls.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

title: 'the Shade of God'
greek: Arabic zill Allah fi'l-ard ('God's shadow on earth')
short: 'Shadow of God on earth' was a traditional title of Muslim sovereigns, which the Ottoman sultans claimed.
body: The title zill Allah, 'the shadow of God (on earth)', was used for caliphs and sultans from the early Islamic centuries, based on a saying attributed to the Prophet that the just ruler is God's shadow on earth, in whom the oppressed take refuge. Ottoman chancery documents applied it to the sultan. The linking couplet of strophe 3 shows Suleyman as a rider thrown when 'the wayward courser, cruel Fate' bolted: the horseman of Time and Space falls, and with him falls the shelter of God's grace. The horse imagery ties back to the charger of strophe 1.

title: Lamenting like the flute
short: The poet asks his heart to wail like the reed-flute (ney), whose lament for separation opens Rumi's Masnavi.
body: The ney, the reed flute, is the classic instrument of lament in the Persianate world, above all because of the opening of Rumi's Masnavi, where the reed cries out for the reed-bed from which it was cut (see the Masnavi prologue in this archive). Baqi's appeal to the heart as fellow-mourner thus makes the elegy a song of separation in the mystical as well as the political sense. The strophe's nature images are precise: hyacinths as 'weeds of woe' (mourning clothes), the rose's petal shaped like an ear (Gibb's note 205), the narcissus, a watchful eye, crying like a night watchman.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Rumi, Masnavi I.1-18 (the Song of the Reed)

title: The king who does not leave his tent
short: The strophe imagines the army waiting for the king to come out of his tent; Suleyman died in his camp before Szigetvar, as Gibb notes.
body: Gibb's note 207 recalls that Sultan Suleyman I died in his camp before Szigeth in Hungary. The historical background sharpens the strophe: the grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha concealed the sultan's death from the army for weeks, until the fortress had fallen and the heir Selim could secure the throne, so the soldiers did wait for a king who would not come out. 'Long have our eyes dwelt on the road, and yet no news hath come' thus records a real anxiety. The pale, dry-lipped king is compared to a rose fallen from the vase.

title: 'the Khusrev of the skies'
short: Khusrev, a Sasanian royal name, means 'king'; the king of the skies is the sun (Gibb's note 208), hiding behind cloud in shame.
body: Khusrev (Persian Khusraw), the name of two Sasanian kings and of the royal lover of Nizami's Khusraw and Shirin, became a general word for a great king. Gibb's note 208 identifies the Khusrev of the skies as the sun, which now goes behind a veil of cloud 'for shame', as if it could not bear to shine after the sultan's light has gone. The conceit links back to the sun of the second strophe and forward to the last strophe, where Selim is a 'Khusrev' whose rising replaces the setting of his father.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

title: Tears as babes
greek: Turkish merdumek ('manikin', the pupil of the eye)
short: Tears are 'babes' born of man; Baqi's curse is that whoever does not weep for the king may have cause to bury his children, his tears.
body: Gibb's note 209 explains that tears are sometimes compared to babes, being sprung from man, perhaps from merdumek, the 'manikin' of the eye; here those babes are to die and be buried, that is, the unsympathising man is to have cause to soak the ground with bitter tears. The couplet is a curse disguised as a prayer, and it shows how far the poem's conceits depend on Turkish and Persian wordplay that Gibb can only explain in notes. Compare the merdum pun in Fuzuli's ghazel in this archive.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

title: The reed-pen tears its collar
short: The mourner tears his collar; the reed-pen, split at its nib, seems to do the same, and the earth rends its garment.
body: Tearing the collar (yaka) of one's shirt was a gesture of extreme grief in Ottoman and Persian culture, as rending garments is in the Hebrew Bible. A reed pen (qalam) is split at the tip, so the poet sees its slit as a torn collar: the very instrument of the elegy mourns. The same strophe makes the sultan's sabre plunge from its sheath into 'the darksome clay', burying itself with its master. This is the linking couplet of the fifth strophe.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Walter G. Andrews, Najaat Black and Mehmet Kalpakli, eds., Ottoman Lyric Poetry: An Anthology (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1997)

title: Idol-temples turned to mosques
short: The sultan converted churches ('idol-temples' to Muslim eyes) into mosques and replaced bells with the call to prayer.
body: Ottoman conquest of a city was symbolised by converting its principal church into a mosque, and church bells, forbidden in Muslim usage, were silenced. To Ottoman poets, churches with their images were butkhane, 'idol-houses'. The sixth strophe praises Suleyman as a ghazi, a warrior for the faith, whose sword 'in cause of God' sacrificed lives. Modern readers will note the triumphalist character of this court poetry; it is the language of the Ottoman ideology of holy war that sustained Suleyman's European campaigns.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Halil Inalcik, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age 1300-1600 (London: Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1973), on Suleyman's last campaign and the succession

title: Ghazi and Shehid
greek: Arabic ghazi ('warrior for the faith') and shahid ('martyr, witness')
short: Suleyman is both ghazi, a victorious warrior of the faith, and shehid, a martyr, because he died on campaign (Gibb's note 210).
body: Gibb's note 210 explains Gazi ve Shehid as 'Muslim conqueror and martyr': both are pleasing to God, since whoever dies in the field against unbelievers is crowned with martyrdom, while the conqueror is rewarded in the next world. He quotes Prince Cantemir's history: the Turks believed Suleyman a favourite of heaven because he died at Szigeth and so became a martyr, and was also a conqueror. 'Eden's flowery, verdant plain' is the martyr's immediate entry to Paradise (Q 3:169).

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Qur'an 3:169

title: Selim's strophe and the 'old man' of Egypt
short: The last strophe greets the new sultan, Selim II; Gibb notes that his line 'The dear old man' should read 'The old Vezir', i.e. Zuleykha's husband in Egypt.
body: Gibb's note 211 says the strophe honours Sultan Selim II, Suleyman's son and successor, and that the third line of his translation is wrong: it should read 'The old Vezir hath passed away from th' Egypt of the world'. The allusion is to the story of Joseph: Zuleykha's husband, the Grand Vizier of Egypt ('Aziz-i Misr), dies, and Joseph rises. Suleyman is the old vizier, Selim the young Joseph, both beautiful and destined to rule. The archive therefore prints Gibb's text with the error he himself identified. Each couplet of the strophe pairs the departed and the new ruler (dawn and sun, Behram and Erdeshir, tiger and lion), with the refrain 'behold!'.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

title: Behram Gur and Erdeshir
short: Behram V, the hunter-king who vanished pursuing a wild ass (gur), stands for Suleyman; gur also means 'grave'. Erdeshir stands for Selim.
body: Gibb's note 212 explains that the Sasanian king Behram V (Bahram Gur, r. 420-38) was famous for hunting the gur or wild ass, and legend said he disappeared in a morass while chasing one. Since gur also means 'tomb' in Persian, poets made an equivoque of it: 'this chase (life) hath at length caused the Behram of the age (Suleyman) to reach the gur'. Erdeshir is the Persian Ardashir, whose Greek form is Artaxerxes. Behram here represents Suleyman, Erdeshir Selim.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
Nizami, Haft Paykar (the story of Bahram Gur)

title: Suleyman's throne and the wind
short: Suleyman bears the name of the prophet-king Solomon, to whom the Qur'an gives command of the wind; now Fate's wind has scattered his throne.
body: In the Qur'an God subjects the wind to Solomon (Sulayman), so that it blows at his command (21:81; 38:36), and Islamic legend has Solomon's throne carried through the air on a carpet borne by the wind. Baqi reverses the miracle: 'the blast of Fate' has blown the throne of this Suleyman to the winds. Iskender's 'couch of might' (compare st. 2) now belongs to Sultan Selim Khan. The couplet thus uses the sultan's name, as Ottoman poets constantly did, to fold him into sacred and legendary history.

sources.cite: Qur'an 21:81 and 38:36
E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215

anchor: The Peacock fair of Eden's mead
title: The Peacock of Eden
short: Suleyman is the Peacock of Paradise, now returned to heaven; Selim is the huma whose shadow brings kingship.
body: Gibb's note 213 recounts the legend that before the Fall the peacock was the most beautiful bird in Paradise, its plumage like pearl and emerald, and its voice so melodious that it was appointed to sing God's praises daily in the streets of heaven; in Islamic tales of the Fall the peacock helps Iblis enter the garden and is expelled with Adam. Baqi's image is purely laudatory: the peacock 'hath soared to Heaven's parterre', returning to its first home, and the huma of happy flight (compare st. 3) now overshadows Selim. The final couplet is the poem's blessing and farewell.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, trans., Ottoman Poems (London: Trubner, 1882), Baqi selection, and notes 196-215
